title: Freaked Out About the First Day of School? Three Quick Things that Help exact publish-time metadata unavailable)
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
source: Dave Stuart Jr. (davestuartjr.com), August 2, 2021 (date estimated from archive ordering;
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. addresses first-day-of-school anxiety through the lens of the Yerkes-Dodson Curve, the century-old psychological finding that performance peaks under moderate pressure rather than too much or too little. He frames managing that internal pressure meter as a genuine professional competency, not a soft-skill nicety, before offering three quick tactics: trivializing the first day when it's warranted, reading a small amount (six pages) of grounding material rather than trying to feel fully prepared, and deliberately relabeling pre-performance anxiety as excitement. The relabeling trick is explained through arousal-state psychology -- nervousness and excitement are both high-arousal states, so it is physiologically easier to shift from nervous to excited than from nervous to calm, which is a lower-arousal state. Stuart backs the excitement reframe with a cited study ("Get Excited: Reappraising Pre-Performance Anxiety as Excitement") and a reference to using the same technique with an anxious student, then invites readers to contribute their own tricks in the comments.
points: The Yerkes-Dodson Curve is used to reframe teacher pressure management as a real, learnable competency underlying long career flourishing, not an incidental soft skill.

The "tell yourself you're excited" trick is grounded in arousal-state psychology: nervousness and excitement are both high-arousal states, making that switch physiologically easier than trying to move straight from nervousness to calm.

Stuart backs the reframe with a specific cited study, "Get Excited: Reappraising Pre-Performance Anxiety as Excitement" in the Journal of Experimental Psychology, rather than presenting it as unverified folk wisdom.

The "read six pages" trick treats partial, bounded preparation as sufficient grounding for the first day, modeling the same satisficing principle Stuart applies elsewhere to grading and lesson planning.
quotes: Since the early 1900s, the consensus in psychology has been that human beings perform best in optimal pressure conditions — not too much pressure, not too little. This is most famously represented in the Yerkes-Dodson Curve.

So to be clear, I'm not babying you when I talk about teacher pressure. It's a big deal. Knowing how to manage it is one of the fundamental competencies beneath long, flourishing careers in education.

Silly Dave — that's not anxiety you're feeling. It's excitement!" This sounds like a pretty stupid thing to say, right? But here's the thing: it works a lot better than stuff like, "Now, Dave, just calm down.

Because nervousness and excitement are both states of high psychological arousal, it's easier to move between them than it is between, say, nervousness and calm. Calm, being a lower state of arousal, is just harder to access when you're worked up.
